title: StarHub to merge with M1, acquire Circles.Life Singapore
html:
StarHub’s merger with M1 is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval by the IMDA.

ST PHOTOS: JASEL POH, AZMI ATHNI

Benjamin Lim

AI generated

SINGAPORE – StarHub will merge with M1 in a deal worth $1.1 billion, the telco announced on Nov 24.

The merger is expected to be completed in the first half of 2027, subject to regulatory approval by the Infocomm Media and Development Authority (IMDA).

Customers will retain their existing plans, services and points of contact, and StarHub and M1 will continue to operate and compete independently until completion, the companies said.

Under the deal, StarHub will pay M1’s shareholders in shares rather than cash. It will issue approximately 651.7 million new shares worth $677.7 million, giving M1’s shareholders a 27.4% take in the enlarged company. M1 will also be sold with $380 million of net debt.

The deal is the latest in a string of acquisitions by StarHub since 2025. The telco fully acquired MyRepublic Broadband in August 2025 and subsequently the company’s mobile business in October 2026. It also migrated subscribers from mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) redONE to its platform in June.

M1’s parent company Keppel had reportedly been looking for another potential buyer for Singapore’s third-largest telco after the merger with Australia-backed telco Simba fell through in May.

IMDA had suspended its review of the deal, which would have been worth $1.4 billion, after it launched an investigation into an alleged breach by Simba.

Simba later admitted to multiple regulatory breaches in November, including the unauthorised use of spectrum for its 4G network.

In a separate filing with the SGX, StarHub also announced that it has exercised its call option to acquire the Singapore operations of Circles.Life, an MVNO which operates on M1’s network.

Together, the combined group will have a customer base of 4.1 million, spanning mobile, broadband, enterprise and digital capabilities.

The proposed consolidation will also mean that the number of telco providers in Singapore will be reduced from four to three, with Singtel and Simba being the other players.

In a statement, StarHub’s outgoing chief executive Nikhil Eapen noted that when Singapore began liberalising the telco market three decades ago, StarHub and M1 gave Singaporeans greater choice and improved industry competitiveness.

“That chapter is now closing,” he said. “Four operators competing for the same mature market will no longer deliver the infrastructure Singapore needs next, and consolidation is the answer.”

Referring to Simba’s failed merger with M1, Eapen told analysts and the media at a briefing that “there are some lessons learnt there” that have shaped StarHub’s approach to seeking regulatory approval from IMDA. He added that StarHub “anticipates and hopes for an efficient and productive regulatory process”.

He said the company will focus on value creation for its shareholders. This includes providing consumers with better product offerings, stronger network coverage and reliable customer experience, as well as continued infrastructure investment for its enterprise businesses.

After the deal is completed, StarHub will prioritise customer retention in 2027 and does not currently plan to make any drastic changes to its operations or price adjustments for its mobile subscription plans, said StarHub CEO-designate Matt Williams, who will take over from Eapen on Jan 1, 2027.

StarHub shareholders will retain 72.6% ownership of the enlarged company at the deal’s completion. Keppel, through its interest in M1’s shareholders, will effectively hold 23% of this interest, with the remaining 4.4% stake held by M1’s other shareholders.

Based on a projected price of $1.50 per StarHub share following the deal’s completion, including cost savings that the companies estimate are worth $1.1 billion from the merger, M1’s enterprise value is estimated to be $1.4 billion.

The deal is estimated to lift StarHub’s revenue for the 12 months ended June 30 to $2.6 billion, and earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) to $500 million.

The telco will keep its dividend policy of 6 cents per share for 2027.

Shareholders are required to approve the deal at separate extraordinary general meetings by the two companies, which are expected to be held in the early part of the first quarter of 2027.

StarHub said it expects the merger to cut annual operating costs by $110 million a year by the 2030 financial year (FY). This is in addition to the $70 million a year that it has committed to reducing by FY 2028, as well as savings of $40 million a year from M1.

The cuts will largely come from reductions in retail presence, infrastructure and IT systems. Williams said that both telcos have thousands of mobile network sites across Singapore, many of which are situated close to one another.

The two telcos already share mobile network infrastructure and antennas across Singapore through their joint venture Antina, which StarHub said will “support integration of spectrum and network assets and faster deployment of network automation and monitoring capabilities”.

Williams added that there are currently no plans to reduce the enlarged company’s headcount, which is around 2,700 employees.

Keppel CEO Loh Chin Hua said the plan at deal completion is for the company to deconsolidate M1, including an estimated net debt of $324 million, of which 10% to 15% will be included in the special dividend calculation for the year.

“As we monetise our stake in the combined entity, we will release substantial capital to fund growth, reduce debt and reward Keppel’s shareholders,” he added.

In a separate briefing with analysts and the media, Loh said that M1’s enterprise information and communications technology business will be retained under the Keppel Technology Solutions arm, which is a core business unit of the company integral to its data centre business.

Keppel will also gain a seat on StarHub’s board as a result of the merger, which Loh said will be crucial to ensuring a smooth transition.
Both Keppel and StarHub requested trading halt before the market opened on Nov 24.
The telco’s share price jumped 4% to $1.05 when trading resumed after the mid-day break and closed at $1.04, while Keppel’s shares briefly rose by 0.5% to $8.87 before falling, closing 4.6% lower at $8.42.
summary: StarHub to merge with M1 in $1.1 billion deal and acquire Circles Life Singapore, subject to regulatory approval. Read more at straitstimes.com.
